items.topic: Where downloaded apps register their running scenarios
items.context: Investigation (round 2) found that `vrooli scenario port` already reads process records from `~/.vrooli/processes/scenarios/<name>/<step>.json` via `internal/app/scenario/service.go::Port()` (lines 223-273) and `internal/scenario/runtime_state.go::RuntimePortBindings()`. Records are written by `internal/lifecycle/phases.go::startTrackedProcess` (lines 350-375) and removed by `lifecycle.Stop()` (lines 515-540). This is the natural leverage point for your suggested direction — bundles register on start/stop, the existing CLI resolver sees them, no new discovery code path is needed. The question is whether bundles should write into the same directory as the host swarm or a sibling directory.

options.label: Reuse the existing `~/.vrooli/processes/scenarios/<name>/` directory; bundles write records with the same schema plus a new `source: "bundle"` field
options.rationale: Single source of truth. The existing CLI resolver reads this path already, so zero new read logic is needed — only a `Source` field on the `Record` struct and a tiebreaker in `Port()` (see D2). Identical shape means `vrooli scenario list`, `vrooli scenario logs` etc. also surface downloaded apps for free. Risk: a downloaded app and the host swarm running the same scenario could interleave records — but that's exactly the scenario precedence (D2) is designed to resolve.

options.label: Parallel directory `~/.vrooli/desktop-apps/<name>/` for bundle records; CLI resolver reads both paths and merges
options.rationale: Physical isolation between swarm-written and bundle-written state. Prevents accidental lifecycle tooling from operating on bundle records. Costs: a second read path in the CLI, duplicate cleanup logic, divergence risk between the two schemas over time.

items.topic: Where to enforce the 'downloaded wins over local swarm' precedence rule
items.context: Your round 1 freeform was 'either in discovery or in the vrooli cli itself.' The investigation shows the CLI does the actual record reading and port resolution; the discovery package is a thin shell-out. Putting the rule in the CLI means every consumer of `packages/api-core/discovery` inherits the correct precedence automatically, and no desktop-specific concepts leak into api-core.

options.label: In the CLI: `internal/app/scenario/service.go::Port()` — after `BuildListPorts`, prefer records where `Source == "bundle"` over `Source == "swarm"` for the same scenario/port
options.rationale: Precedence is a property of resolution, not a property of the caller. All discovery-package consumers benefit without changes. Tests can hit the CLI directly with a synthetic record dir. No api-core coupling to desktop concepts.

options.label: In the resolver: `packages/api-core/discovery/resolve.go` reads the record directory itself and short-circuits before shelling out
options.rationale: Avoids a subprocess for the common case (fast). But couples api-core to desktop registry shape, duplicates logic the CLI already has, and any future schema change breaks two places.

options.label: Both layers — defense in depth (resolver checks registry, CLI also enforces precedence)
options.rationale: Most defensive. Also the most places to maintain and the most places to diverge.

items.topic: Staleness handling for records left by crashed bundles
items.context: If a downloaded app crashes without the chance to deregister, its record remains on disk with a stale PID and (possibly) a port that nobody is listening on. The resolver would return a dead endpoint. The host swarm lifecycle currently relies on graceful stop + port locks for cleanup; bundles need an equivalent. The contract must specify the strategy so the regression suite (`execute/desktop-ecosystem-interop-regression-coverage`) can verify it.

options.label: Reader-side liveness check: when `Port()` reads a record, verify the PID is alive (kill -0 / Windows equivalent) before returning its port; skip dead records, ideally removing them
options.rationale: Cheapest, no background goroutine inside bundles, cross-platform via existing Go process APIs, self-healing (dead records get garbage-collected on the next read). Risk: PID reuse — a long-stale record whose PID was recycled could accidentally look alive. Mitigation: also compare `StartedAt` against process start time when available.

options.label: TTL heartbeat: bundles touch their record file every N seconds; readers treat records older than 2*N as stale
options.rationale: Simple and cross-platform, but requires a background ticker in every bundle that can reliably run even under heavy load, and readers have to do time-based comparisons (clock skew considerations). Extra writes on SSD/disk budgets.

options.label: Lock-file / flock approach: register with an OS-held lock so the kernel cleans it up when the bundle exits (for any reason)
options.rationale: Automatic cleanup on crash is the main appeal. But cross-platform lock semantics are inconsistent (Windows exclusive opens vs Unix advisory flock), and the record file itself cannot be the lock because readers need to read it freely.

items.topic: How the bundle shim resolves peers (other downloaded apps or the host swarm)
items.context: Today the bundle shim in `scenarios/scenario-to-desktop/api/bundle/staging.go` only resolves services inside its own `bundle.json`. For peer-downloaded-app or downloaded-app → local-swarm calls to work, the shim must consult the shared registry from D1. Two clean paths exist: the shim reads the registry itself, or the shim falls through to a host `vrooli` binary (if one is on PATH) which reads the registry. Round 1 settled that Windows gets a compiled `vrooli.exe` helper (D3=A).

options.label: Shim reads the shared registry directly for unknown scenario names (bash shim adds a small registry-read path on Unix; Windows compiled helper handles it natively)
options.rationale: No dependency on a host Vrooli install being present — works uniformly on hosts that have never seen the Vrooli CLI. Matches the 'one coherent ecosystem' goal on any desktop. Cost: the Unix bash shim's python3 dependency grows a bit (still reading JSON, same pattern as today).

options.label: Shim shells to the host `vrooli` binary on PATH (after the shim itself) for unknown names; fails gracefully if no host vrooli exists
options.rationale: Reuses the CLI's resolution entirely, zero duplication. But makes inter-bundle discovery depend on a host Vrooli install, which contradicts the coherent-ecosystem goal on clean desktops.

options.label: Hybrid: shim reads registry for a live record; falls back to host `vrooli` if no record and a host binary exists
options.rationale: Maximum robustness. But the most code paths to maintain and test, and the two branches can drift in subtle ways.

items.text: Major reframing: `vrooli scenario port` ALREADY reads a file-based process registry at `~/.vrooli/processes/scenarios/<name>/*.json` (see `internal/app/scenario/service.go:223-273` and `internal/scenario/runtime_state.go:109-147`). No new registry layer is required — downloaded apps can participate by writing the same record shape on start and removing it on stop. This is the core leverage point of the emerging contract.

Process record schema at `internal/process/process.go:17-30` already contains PID, PGID, Port, Scenario, Step, StartedAt, Status. Adding one optional `Source` field (values `"swarm"` | `"bundle"`) would let the resolver distinguish origins without breaking existing readers. Registration on bundle start maps 1:1 to `process.WriteScenarioRecord`; deregistration maps to `process.RemoveScenarioRecord`.

`~/.vrooli/` is hardcoded throughout `internal/config/config.go` — there is no XDG_STATE_HOME support today, and the same path is used on Windows (via `os.UserHomeDir()`). The registry reader in bundles should use the same `HomeDir()` resolver the CLI uses so the bundle and the host always look at the same location. Moving to XDG-native paths can be a follow-up, not a blocker.

The host swarm lifecycle already handles crash-time cleanup for its own records via port locks (`internal/lifecycle/lifecycle.go:515-540`). Bundle-written records will sit outside that lifecycle unless they reuse the same cleanup primitives or the resolver applies a liveness check (D3=A). Without a strategy, stale bundle records will accumulate and the regression suite will see flaky 'dead endpoint' results.
